Overview

Trinidad and Tobago at a Glance

Trinidad and Tobago is a twin-island republic with a common-law legal system, final appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council and the most industrialised economy in the English-speaking Caribbean. Its legal framework is extensive on paper but uneven in practice. The Data Protection Act 2011 has been only partly proclaimed, the private security and investigation industry lacks an overarching licensing statute, and the US State Department describes the courts as independent but slow, with a large backlog. Company records are available through the Registrar General's online Companies Registry, while beneficial ownership returns introduced in 2019 and amended in 2024 are accessible to competent authorities.

Organisations commission work involving Trinidad and Tobago mainly because of its oil, natural gas, liquefied natural gas and petrochemical industries, which have historically attracted most foreign direct investment, and the large network of contractors, service companies and suppliers around them. Typical needs include due diligence on joint venture partners, agents and subcontractors, integrity checks connected to public procurement and state enterprises, inquiries into procurement fraud, employee misconduct and theft of materials, and asset tracing for judgments and insolvencies. Manufacturers, shippers, banks and insurers also seek research on regional counterparties, and proximity to Venezuela means some matters require careful sanctions screening.

Legal Environment

How the law shapes investigative work involving Trinidad and Tobago

Legal system

Trinidad and Tobago has a common-law system derived from English law. The Supreme Court of Judicature comprises the High Court of Justice, which hears civil claims above the Magistrates' Courts' limit, and the Court of Appeal, with final appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. Domestic arbitration is governed by the Arbitration Act of 1939, and foreign awards are enforced under the Arbitration (Foreign Arbitral Awards) Act 1996. The Dispute Resolution Centre in Port of Spain offers arbitration and mediation. Court delays are significant, so interim relief and settlement strategy often matter more than trial dates.

Data protection

Data Protection Act, 2011 (partially proclaimed) · Regulator: Office of the Information Commissioner (provided for under the Act)

Only parts of the Data Protection Act 2011 have been proclaimed, beginning in January 2012. The General Privacy Principles in section 6 are in force and apply to anyone handling personal information: collection with the individual's knowledge and consent, use limited to the identified purpose, accuracy, security and openness. Sensitive personal information generally requires consent unless an exception applies. Section 6 also states that personal information should leave the country only where the recipient jurisdiction offers comparable safeguards, though no list of such countries has been published. The detailed obligations for private organisations and the enforcement provisions are not yet in force, so investigative work is scoped to the principles and to the client's own law.

Private investigators

We have not identified a dedicated licensing statute for private investigators in Trinidad and Tobago. Security firms require approval, with the Commissioner of Police deciding on licences, and protective service agencies employing precepted officers register with the Ministry of National Security. A 2014 draft Private Security Industry Bill would create a Private Security Services Authority to license the sector, including private investigators, but we have not confirmed that it has been enacted. Private investigators have no special powers: police, tax, immigration and banking records are not available to private parties, and surveillance and recording must respect criminal law and constitutional privacy protections.

Corporate & public records

Companies are registered with the Companies Registry of the Registrar General's Department, Ministry of Legal Affairs, which offers an online search of company details and filings; registration is handled through the TTBizLink platform. The Companies (Amendment) Act 2019 introduced beneficial ownership registers and returns, and amendments in force from September 2024 extended the regime; FIUTT guidance describes the information as accessible to competent authorities. The extractive sector has a separate EITI beneficial ownership disclosure register launched in 2020. Nearly 80 percent of land remains under the older common-law deeds system rather than the Real Property Act register.

Anti-corruption & AML

The Prevention of Corruption Act criminalises bribery involving public bodies, and the Integrity in Public Life Act requires asset declarations by public officials and established the Integrity Commission. The Freedom of Information Act provides access to official documents subject to exemptions, and procurement legislation has recently been implemented. The Proceeds of Crime Act 2000 underpins money laundering offences, with the Financial Intelligence Unit of Trinidad and Tobago (FIUTT) receiving suspicious transaction reports and supervising certain non-regulated businesses.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters Touching Trinidad and Tobago

TDSC begins each Trinidad and Tobago engagement with a jurisdictional review: the client's purpose, which records are public through the Companies Registry and the courts, which are restricted to competent authorities, and how the partly proclaimed Data Protection Act and the client's own law apply. Desk research from Nashville draws on registry filings, judgments, Gazette notices, energy sector disclosures and Trinidadian media. Because there is no settled licensing regime for private investigators, TDSC is selective about the local professionals it coordinates, checks their standing and methods, and works through the client's Trinidadian counsel for interviews, approaches to witnesses and any court applications. Personal data is minimised and transferred securely, and every matter with Venezuelan or other sanctions links is screened before acceptance.

TDSC has no office in Trinidad and Tobago. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope. TDSC does not provide legal advice.

Typical Matters

Where Investigative Work Involving Trinidad and Tobago Concentrates

01

Energy sector partner due diligence

Background research on joint venture partners, agents, contractors and service companies in upstream oil and gas, LNG and petrochemicals at Point Lisas and elsewhere, covering ownership, litigation, regulatory history, political exposure and reputation before contracts, acquisitions or renewals.

02

Procurement and supplier integrity

Integrity checks on suppliers and intermediaries bidding for work with state enterprises and ministries, including conflicts of interest, related-party links and prior disputes, supporting compliance teams that must demonstrate reasonable diligence under anti-bribery laws in their home jurisdictions.

03

Fraud and misconduct inquiries

Supporting internal investigations into procurement fraud, kickbacks, diversion of materials and employee misconduct at plants, yards and operating sites, through document review, public-record research and lawful interviews coordinated with Trinidadian counsel and, where necessary, qualified local professionals.

04

Asset tracing and judgment enforcement

Identifying companies, property and business interests connected to judgment debtors or insolvent counterparties, taking account of the dual land system and slow court processes, and preparing material that counsel can use to seek freezing orders or enforce foreign judgments and awards.

05

Regional counterparty and sanctions research

Research on shipping, trading and logistics counterparties operating between Trinidad and Tobago, Venezuela, Guyana and the wider Caribbean, identifying ownership links, vessel and trade histories and sanctions exposure so clients can make informed compliance decisions.

Questions

Trinidad and Tobago: Frequently Asked Questions

Are private investigators licensed in Trinidad and Tobago?

We have not identified a dedicated licensing statute. Security firms need approval from the Commissioner of Police, and a draft Private Security Industry Bill from 2014 would bring private investigators within a licensing authority, but we have not confirmed its enactment. TDSC therefore vets any local professional carefully and works through Trinidadian counsel on method and scope.

Is the Data Protection Act 2011 fully in force?

No. Only parts were proclaimed from January 2012, including the General Privacy Principles, which apply to anyone handling personal information. The detailed obligations for private organisations and much of the enforcement machinery have not been brought into force. TDSC treats the principles as binding in practice and applies data minimisation and secure handling throughout.

Can TDSC identify the beneficial owners of a Trinidadian company?

Beneficial ownership returns are lodged with the Companies Registry and are described in official guidance as accessible to competent authorities, not as a public register. TDSC builds ownership pictures from company filings, the energy sector EITI disclosures where relevant, litigation records and media, and counsel can advise on formal disclosure routes.

Why do energy companies commission due diligence in Trinidad and Tobago?

Energy remains the dominant sector, and operators rely on networks of agents, contractors and local partners, some with ties to state enterprises. Foreign companies subject to US, UK or other anti-bribery laws need evidence that they checked those relationships. TDSC provides documented, source-based findings that compliance and legal teams can rely on.

Is verifying land ownership straightforward?

Often not. Nearly 80 percent of land is held under the older common-law deeds system, which requires tracing chains of title rather than checking a single register, and foreign investors need a licence to acquire more than five acres. Title work is done by Trinidadian attorneys, which TDSC complements with research on owners and prior disputes.
